title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
hookLine: in a book of ruins: his mercies are new every morning

lines: A LINE OF HOPE IN THE MIDDLE.
cards: Jerusalem has fallen. The Babylonian army has broken through the walls, burned the Temple, and marched much of the city's population away. Streets that were full are empty.

Children faint from hunger at the corners. The roads to the city mourn, the text says, because no one comes to the feasts anymore. Someone sat in that ruin and wrote five poems about it: the book of Lamentations.
Raw grief, long stretches of pain, no tidy answers. And right in the middle of the middle poem, a line hopeful enough to end up in a hymn.

teach.b: Just before it, the poet is at the bottom. He's been walled in, his prayers shut out; he's forgotten what happiness is. Then he calls something to mind, and hope rises.
In the King James Bible: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Notice what he doesn't say.
The city isn't rebuilt. The grief isn't over; it goes on for two more chapters. One thing hasn't run out: God's mercies.
The Hebrew word is chesed, steadfast loving-kindness.

New every morning: not stored up from yesterday, not a fixed supply that gets used up, but delivered fresh, like the manna in the desert that had to be gathered each day. The book's shape holds a detail too.

Four of the five poems are acrostics, each verse or stanza starting with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The third poem, where this line sits, triples it: three verses for every letter, sixty-six in all.

teach.h: GRIEF IN ORDER, LETTER BY LETTER.
teach.b: Grief put in order, letter by letter, as if to say: we will grieve this completely. And at the center of it, this. The author isn't named in the text; an old tradition credits the prophet Jeremiah.
Jewish communities read Lamentations each year on Tisha B'Av, mourning the Temple's fall.
And a Methodist writer named Thomas Chisholm later drew on this line for the hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness.

how: Many Christians sing the hymn Great Is Thy Faithfulness, drawn from Lamentations 3:22–23, and some read the verses at the start of the day; in Jewish practice the whole book of Lamentations is chanted on Tisha B'Av.

games.q: you're a poet sitting in a burned city. you've said everything about the pain. what comes next?
o: stop writing: there's nothing more to say.
call one thing to mind: God's mercies are new every morning.
games.why: he calls something to mind, and hope rises: "they are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." the ruin is still there. the mercy is new anyway.

practice: Think of the ruin in your own week, a mistake you made, a hurt you carried, a thing that didn't get fixed, and don't pretend it isn't there; the poet didn't.
Then picture tomorrow morning, light coming in, the first breath of the day, and imagine waking without dragging today's weight into it, not because it's solved, but because the morning is new.
If you pray, you can say the line itself: great is thy faithfulness.

wordCard.voice: Chesed. Hebrew for steadfast loving-kindness, the mercy Lamentations says doesn't run out in a ruined city, but comes fresh each day, new every morning.
